1.title: Clinical Pharmacy — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a core principle of antimicrobial stewardship?
options: Selecting the narrowest-spectrum agent based on local susceptibility data
Minimizing duration of therapy to the shortest effective course
Using combination therapy for all severe infections to prevent resistance
Implementing formulary restrictions to limit broad-spectrum use
questions.answer: Using combination therapy for all severe infections to prevent resistance
questions.explanation: Combination therapy is not routinely required for all severe infections; it should be reserved for specific indications such as tuberculosis or neutropenic sepsis.

questions.stem: An antibiogram is most useful for guiding therapy by providing:
options: Susceptibility patterns of pathogens isolated from individual patients
Antimicrobial resistance trends within a specific healthcare facility
Pharmacokinetic data of antimicrobial agents in critically ill patients
Cost-effectiveness analysis of different antimicrobial regimens
questions.answer: Antimicrobial resistance trends within a specific healthcare facility
questions.explanation: An antibiogram aggregates susceptibility data from a healthcare facility to guide empiric therapy choices based on local resistance patterns.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of penicillin allergy develops anaphylaxis when challenged with a cephalosporin. Which mechanism best explains this cross-reactivity?
options: Shared beta-lactam ring structure leading to IgE-mediated hypersensitivity
Presence of identical side chains in both drug classes
Inhibition of renal excretion causing toxic accumulation
Disruption of gut microbiota leading to hypersensitivity reactions
questions.answer: Shared beta-lactam ring structure leading to IgE-mediated hypersensitivity
questions.explanation: Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is primarily due to the shared beta-lactam ring, which can trigger IgE-mediated allergic reactions in sensitized individuals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST common cause of community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospitalization?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the most frequent bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia worldwide, accounting for the majority of hospitalized cases.

questions.stem: A patient with atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae fails to improve on doxycycline. Which alternative agent should be considered?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a cell wall and is inherently resistant to beta-lactams; macrolides such as azithromycin are the preferred agents.

questions.stem: Which laboratory finding is MOST indicative of hepatotoxicity secondary to anti-tuberculosis therapy?
options: Serum ALT >3 times the upper limit of normal with symptoms
Isolated elevation of serum bilirubin without enzyme changes
Mild elevation of alkaline phosphatase with normal ALT
Elevated serum creatinine with normal liver enzymes
questions.answer: Serum ALT >3 times the upper limit of normal with symptoms
questions.explanation: Hepatotoxicity from anti-TB drugs is typically defined as ALT or AST >3 times ULN with symptoms, or >5 times ULN without symptoms.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a recommended strategy to prevent antimicrobial resistance?
questions.explanation: Antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections and their unnecessary use contributes directly to antimicrobial resistance.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected Legionella pneumonia should be empirically treated with:
questions.explanation: Legionella species are intracellular pathogens not covered by beta-lactams; fluoroquinolones or macrolides are the preferred agents.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the primary mechanism of action of isoniazid in tuberculosis therapy?
options: Inhibition of mycobacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.answer: Inhibition of mycobacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.explanation: Isoniazid inhibits the synthesis of mycolic acids, essential components of the mycobacterial cell wall, through inhibition of the enzyme InhA.

questions.stem: A patient with a positive tuberculin skin test but no clinical or radiographic evidence of active disease has:
options: No need for further evaluation or treatment
A false-positive result due to prior BCG vaccination
questions.explanation: A positive tuberculin skin test with no evidence of active disease indicates latent tuberculosis infection, which requires treatment to prevent reactivation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy for a patient with hospital-acquired pneumonia in a facility with high rates of MRSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
questions.explanation: Empiric therapy for hospital-acquired pneumonia in settings with high MRSA and Pseudomonas rates should cover both organisms until culture results are available.

questions.stem: Which of the following adverse effects is MOST specific to ethambutol therapy?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol is associated with dose-dependent optic neuritis, which can lead to visual disturbances and requires regular monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient with a confirmed diagnosis of tuberculosis develops jaundice after 2 weeks of therapy. Which is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Stop all anti-TB drugs and rechallenge sequentially once LFTs normalize
Switch to a non-hepatotoxic regimen such as streptomycin and ethambutol
questions.answer: Stop all anti-TB drugs and rechallenge sequentially once LFTs normalize
questions.explanation: All first-line anti-TB drugs are potentially hepatotoxic; stopping all drugs and rechallenging sequentially is the safest approach to identify the culprit.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea?
questions.explanation: Clostridioides difficile is the leading cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis due to disruption of normal gut flora.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of the CURB-65 score used to assess severity of community-acquired pneumonia?
questions.explanation: CURB-65 includes Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30 breaths/min, Blood pressure <90/60 mmHg, and age ≥65 years.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin is diagnosed with bacterial endocarditis caused by viridans group streptococci. Which is the MOST appropriate alternative agent?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is the preferred alternative for patients with severe penicillin allergy requiring coverage for gram-positive organisms such as viridans group streptococci.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate monitoring parameter for a patient receiving prolonged therapy with vancomycin?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is nephrotoxic; serum creatinine should be monitored regularly, especially in patients receiving prolonged therapy or with risk factors for renal impairment.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the treatment of tuberculosis in pregnancy?
options: Streptomycin is the preferred agent due to its safety profile
Rifampicin should be avoided due to teratogenic effects
Isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol are considered safe
Pyrazinamide is contraindicated in all trimesters
questions.answer: Isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol are considered safe
questions.explanation: Isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol are considered safe in pregnancy; pyrazinamide may be used but is not routinely recommended in some guidelines.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of aspiration pneumonia should be empirically treated to cover which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonia often involves mixed aerobic and anaerobic flora from the oral cavity; coverage for anaerobes is essential.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to prevent the emergence of resistance during tuberculosis treatment?
options: Administering all doses under direct observation
Using high-dose monotherapy to ensure bacterial kill
Shortening the duration of therapy to 3 months
Adding a second agent only when resistance is confirmed
questions.answer: Administering all doses under direct observation
questions.explanation: Directly observed therapy (DOT) ensures adherence and reduces the risk of resistance development by preventing incomplete treatment courses.

questions.stem: A patient with a confirmed diagnosis of Legionella pneumonia fails to improve on azithromycin. Which is the MOST appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Legionella species may develop resistance to macrolides; fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin are the preferred alternative agents.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST common adverse effect of rifampicin therapy?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin commonly causes orange-red discoloration of urine, tears, sweat, and other body fluids due to its metabolism and excretion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a recommended strategy for antimicrobial de-escalation?
options: Switching from broad-spectrum to narrow-spectrum agents based on culture results
Reducing the dose of the antimicrobial to minimize toxicity
Stopping unnecessary combination therapy once a pathogen is identified
Shortening the duration of therapy based on clinical response
questions.answer: Reducing the dose of the antimicrobial to minimize toxicity
questions.explanation: De-escalation focuses on narrowing spectrum and shortening duration, not simply reducing dose, which may compromise efficacy.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis has a positive Gram stain showing gram-negative diplococci. Which is the MOST likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Gram-negative diplococci on cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain are characteristic of Neisseria meningitidis, a common cause of bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy for a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis in an immunocompetent adult?
questions.explanation: Empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis in adults should cover Streptococcus pneumoniae (including penicillin-resistant strains) and Neisseria meningitidis; ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is recommended.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST common adverse effect of pyrazinamide therapy?
questions.explanation: Pyrazinamide is associated with hepatotoxicity, which is dose-dependent and requires regular monitoring of liver function tests.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of tuberculosis develops peripheral neuropathy after 4 weeks of therapy. Which is the MOST likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid is associated with peripheral neuropathy due to pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency; co-administration of pyridoxine is recommended to prevent this.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to prevent antimicrobial resistance in a healthcare facility?
options: Implementing formulary restrictions to limit broad-spectrum agents
Routine use of combination therapy for all infections
Prescribing antibiotics for all febrile patients
Using the most expensive agents to ensure efficacy
questions.answer: Implementing formulary restrictions to limit broad-spectrum agents
questions.explanation: Formulary restrictions and antimicrobial stewardship programs are key strategies to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use and prevent resistance.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of bacterial endocarditis caused by Enterococcus faecalis is allergic to penicillin. Which is the MOST appropriate alternative agent?
questions.explanation: Enterococcus faecalis is inherently resistant to cephalosporins; vancomycin is the preferred alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate monitoring parameter for a patient receiving prolonged therapy with isoniazid?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid can cause pyridoxine deficiency leading to peripheral neuropathy; monitoring vitamin B6 levels and supplementation is recommended.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia fails to improve on amoxicillin-clavulanate. Which is the MOST likely reason?
options: Infection with an atypical organism such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Infection with a gram-negative organism such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa
questions.answer: Infection with an atypical organism such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin-clavulanate does not cover atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which are common causes of community-acquired pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to prevent the spread of antimicrobial resistance in a community setting?
options: Prescribing antibiotics for all patients with fever
Educating patients on the appropriate use of antibiotics
Limiting the duration of therapy to 3 days for all infections
questions.answer: Educating patients on the appropriate use of antibiotics
questions.explanation: Patient education on appropriate antibiotic use is a key strategy to reduce unnecessary prescriptions and prevent resistance in the community.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of tuberculosis develops visual disturbances after 6 weeks of therapy. Which is the MOST likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol is associated with optic neuritis, which can cause visual disturbances such as blurred vision or color blindness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy for a patient with suspected aspiration pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonia often involves mixed aerobic and anaerobic flora; ampicillin-sulbactam provides coverage for both gram-positive and anaerobic organisms.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis has a positive cerebrospinal fluid culture for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Which is the MOST appropriate definitive therapy?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is typically susceptible to ceftriaxone, which is the preferred agent for definitive therapy in bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to prevent antimicrobial resistance in a patient with recurrent urinary tract infections?
options: Educating the patient on appropriate hygiene measures
Limiting fluid intake to reduce urinary frequency
questions.answer: Educating the patient on appropriate hygiene measures
questions.explanation: Patient education on hygiene measures and avoiding unnecessary antibiotic use is key to preventing recurrent urinary tract infections and resistance.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of tuberculosis develops hyperuricemia after 2 weeks of therapy. Which is the MOST likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Pyrazinamide is associated with hyperuricemia due to its effect on purine metabolism; monitoring uric acid levels is recommended.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate monitoring parameter for a patient receiving prolonged therapy with rifampicin?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin can cause hematologic adverse effects such as thrombocytopenia; regular monitoring of CBC is recommended during prolonged therapy.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of bacterial endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus is allergic to penicillin. Which is the MOST appropriate alternative agent?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant strains, is typically susceptible to vancomycin, which is the preferred alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to prevent antimicrobial resistance in a healthcare facility?
options: Using the most expensive agents to ensure efficacy
Prescribing antibiotics for all febrile patients
Routine use of combination therapy for all infections
questions.explanation: Antimicrobial stewardship programs are designed to optimize antibiotic use, reduce resistance, and improve patient outcomes in healthcare facilities.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of tuberculosis develops arthralgia after 3 weeks of therapy. Which is the MOST likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Pyrazinamide is associated with arthralgia and hyperuricemia due to its effect on purine metabolism; symptoms typically resolve with discontinuation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy for a patient with suspected hospital-acquired pneumonia in a facility with high rates of MRSA?
questions.explanation: Empiric therapy for hospital-acquired pneumonia in settings with high MRSA rates should cover both gram-negative organisms (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa) and MRSA.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis has a positive cerebrospinal fluid culture for Neisseria meningitidis. Which is the MOST appropriate definitive therapy?
questions.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis is typically susceptible to ceftriaxone, which is the preferred agent for definitive therapy in bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to prevent antimicrobial resistance in a patient with a history of recurrent skin and soft tissue infections?
options: Educating the patient on appropriate wound care and hygiene
Limiting fluid intake to reduce systemic inflammation
questions.answer: Educating the patient on appropriate wound care and hygiene
questions.explanation: Patient education on wound care and hygiene measures is key to preventing recurrent skin and soft tissue infections and reducing the need for antibiotics.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of tuberculosis develops gastrointestinal upset after 1 week of therapy. Which is the MOST likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin commonly causes gastrointestinal upset, including nausea and vomiting, due to its effect on the gastrointestinal mucosa.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate monitoring parameter for a patient receiving prolonged therapy with ethambutol?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol is associated with optic neuritis; regular monitoring of visual acuity and color vision is essential to detect early signs of toxicity.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of bacterial endocarditis caused by viridans group streptococci is allergic to penicillin. Which is the MOST appropriate alternative agent?
questions.explanation: Viridans group streptococci are typically susceptible to vancomycin, which is the preferred alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to prevent antimicrobial resistance in a community pharmacy setting?
options: Educating patients on the appropriate use of antibiotics
Limiting the duration of therapy to 3 days for all infections
questions.answer: Educating patients on the appropriate use of antibiotics
questions.explanation: Patient education on appropriate antibiotic use is a key strategy to reduce unnecessary prescriptions and prevent resistance in the community.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of tuberculosis develops rash after 2 weeks of therapy. Which is the MOST likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid is associated with hypersensitivity reactions, including rash, due to its effect on the immune system.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy for a patient with suspected atypical pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Atypical pneumonia is commonly caused by organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Legionella species, which are not covered by beta-lactams; macrolides such as azithromycin are preferred.

questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis has a positive cerebrospinal fluid culture for Listeria monocytogenes. Which is the MOST appropriate definitive therapy?
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is inherently resistant to cephalosporins; ampicillin plus gentamicin is the preferred regimen for definitive therapy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to prevent antimicrobial resistance in a patient with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections?
options: Educating the patient on appropriate hygiene measures
Limiting fluid intake to reduce urinary frequency
questions.answer: Educating the patient on appropriate hygiene measures
questions.explanation: Patient education on hygiene measures and avoiding unnecessary antibiotic use is key to preventing recurrent urinary tract infections and resistance.

questions.stem: List four minor manifestations used in the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever according to the Jones criteria.
questions.modelAnswer: 1. Fever; 2. Arthralgia; 3. Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP); 4. Prolonged PR interval on electrocardiogram.

questions.stem: Describe four symptoms and signs that should raise suspicion of pharyngitis of viral etiology.
questions.modelAnswer: 1. Cough; 2. Rhinorrhea; 3. Conjunctivitis; 4. Absence of fever or presence of low-grade fever; 5. Presence of viral exanthem or enanthem.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old patient with a positive history of treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis 5 years ago presents to the chest clinic with malaise for 3 weeks, night sweats, and unintended weight loss. Sputum GeneXpert tests positive for rifampicin-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Identify the diagnosis and design a five-drug treatment plan for this patient.
questions.modelAnswer: Diagnosis: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Treatment plan: 1. Levofloxacin; 2. Ethionamide; 3. Cycloserine; 4. Pyrazinamide; 5. Ethambutol. Duration: 18–24 months, with at least 6 months of injectable agents if tolerated.

questions.stem: Describe any six core elements of establishing an antimicrobial stewardship program.
questions.modelAnswer: 1. Leadership commitment; 2. Accountability; 3. Pharmacy expertise; 4. Action (e.g., preauthorization, prospective audit and feedback); 5. Tracking (monitoring antibiotic prescribing and resistance patterns); 6. Reporting (regular feedback to providers); 7. Education (training on appropriate antibiotic use).

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department with confusion, vomiting, headache, and neck stiffness. Temperature is 39.0°C, pulse 117/min, respiratory rate 14/min, and blood pressure 94/56 mmHg. Examination reveals lethargy, disorientation, nuchal rigidity, and petechial rash on extremities that progresses to purpura within 24 hours. Identify the most probable diagnosis and causative agent. Justify your answer. Describe three investigations to support the diagnosis. Review five patient-related factors to consider when selecting empirical antimicrobial therapy. Propose an appropriate treatment plan. List two complications to monitor. Explain how you would manage contacts.

modelAnswer.causative_agent: Neisseria meningitidis (serogroup C most likely in outbreaks).
modelAnswer.justification: Clinical presentation with fever, confusion, nuchal rigidity, and petechial rash progressing to purpura is classic for meningococcal disease. The rapid progression and systemic involvement suggest meningococcemia.
modelAnswer.investigations: 1. Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis (cell count, Gram stain, culture, PCR); 2. Blood cultures; 3. Skin lesion biopsy for Gram stain and culture.
modelAnswer.patient_factors: 1. Age and immune status (young adults in close contact settings are high risk); 2. Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia); 3. Renal function (risk of acute kidney injury); 4. Coagulation status (risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation); 5. Allergy history (e.g., penicillin allergy).
modelAnswer.treatment_plan: 1. Immediate empiric therapy: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h (or benzylpenicillin 2.4g IV q4h if no allergy); 2. Supportive care: Fluid resuscitation, vasopressors if needed, and close monitoring in ICU; 3. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts: Rifampicin 600mg PO q12h for 2 days or ciprofloxacin 500mg PO single dose.
modelAnswer.complications: 1. Septic shock with multi-organ failure; 2. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
modelAnswer.contact_management: Identify and provide chemoprophylaxis to close contacts (household members, intimate contacts, healthcare workers with direct exposure to respiratory secretions). Use rifampicin or ciprofloxacin as above. Vaccination should be considered for serogroup-specific outbreaks.

questions.stem: Mr. JW, a 40-year-old previously healthy man, presents 5 days after returning from a conference abroad with sudden onset of fever, cough producing rusty sputum, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and disorientation. His respiratory rate is 33/min, SpO2 85%, temperature 38.8°C, blood pressure 100/68 mmHg, and pulse 110/min. Urea is 8.5 mmol/L. Identify the most likely diagnosis and causative organism. Justify your answer. Outline two additional investigations. Evaluate whether he should be treated as an outpatient, inpatient (general ward), or in the ICU. Formulate a treatment plan. Describe how you would monitor for response to treatment.

modelAnswer.causative_organism: Streptococcus pneumoniae (most likely) or Legionella pneumophila (given travel history and whirlpool exposure).
modelAnswer.justification: Sudden onset of fever, rusty sputum, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxia are classic for pneumococcal pneumonia. Travel history and whirlpool exposure increase the likelihood of Legionella, which can present similarly with systemic symptoms.
modelAnswer.investigations: 1. Chest X-ray (to confirm pneumonia and assess for complications such as effusion or multilobar involvement); 2. Sputum Gram stain and culture, urinary antigen test for Legionella and pneumococcus.
modelAnswer.care_setting: Inpatient in the ICU due to severe sepsis (hypotension, hypoxia, tachycardia, altered mental status, and elevated urea). CURB-65 score would likely be ≥3, mandating ICU admission.
modelAnswer.treatment_plan: 1. Empiric therapy: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h plus azithromycin 500mg IV q24h (covers both pneumococcus and atypical organisms); 2. Supportive care: Oxygen therapy to maintain SpO2 >90%, fluid resuscitation, and close monitoring; 3. Consider vasopressors if hypotension persists.
modelAnswer.monitoring: 1. Clinical parameters: Temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and mental status; 2. Laboratory parameters: White blood cell count, C-reactive protein, and arterial blood gases; 3. Radiographic parameters: Chest X-ray to assess for improvement or complications; 4. Microbiological parameters: Follow-up sputum cultures and urinary antigen tests if initially positive.

2.title: Clinical Pharmacy — Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of COPD and recent hospitalization for exacerbation is admitted with suspected hospital-acquired pneumonia. Local antibiogram data shows 30% resistance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa to piperacillin-tazobactam. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy choice based on antimicrobial stewardship principles?
questions.explanation: Local antibiogram data supports piperacillin-tazobactam as empiric therapy for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, with de-escalation guided by culture results; adding vancomycin is unnecessary without MRSA risk.

questions.stem: A hospital’s antibiotic formulary restricts the use of carbapenems to culture-proven infections with multidrug-resistant organisms. Which of the following is the PRIMARY goal of this formulary restriction?
options: To minimize the development of carbapenem resistance
To increase the use of narrow-spectrum agents
questions.answer: To minimize the development of carbapenem resistance
questions.explanation: Carbapenem restriction is a core antimicrobial stewardship strategy to preserve the utility of these agents by reducing selective pressure for resistance.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old female with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections presents with fever and flank pain. Urine culture grows ESBL-producing Escherichia coli. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate oral step-down therapy after clinical improvement?
questions.explanation: Nitrofurantoin achieves high urinary concentrations and is active against ESBL-producing E. coli; fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX are less reliable due to resistance.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a documented anaphylactic reaction to penicillin is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. Sputum Gram stain shows gram-positive diplococci. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin provides coverage for Streptococcus pneumoniae in penicillin-allergic patients without cross-reactivity; cefazolin and vancomycin are not first-line for CAP.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female with a 5-day history of fever, cough, and myalgia is diagnosed with atypical pneumonia. Which of the following organisms is MOST likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a common cause of atypical pneumonia characterized by gradual onset, non-productive cough, and extrapulmonary symptoms.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male with COPD exacerbation is started on empiric therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. On day 3, he develops profuse watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone is a high-risk agent for C. difficile infection; symptoms of profuse diarrhea and abdominal cramping are classic for this complication.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male with a history of alcohol use disorder is started on standard four-drug therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis (RHZE). Baseline LFTs are ALT 35 U/L and AST 40 U/L. Which of the following increases his risk of hepatotoxicity?
questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol use is a major risk factor for isoniazid- and rifampicin-induced hepatotoxicity due to impaired drug metabolism and hepatic reserve.

questions.stem: A patient with active tuberculosis develops jaundice and elevated bilirubin after 2 weeks of RHZE therapy. LFTs show ALT 250 U/L and total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate management step?
options: Continue all TB medications and monitor closely
Stop all TB medications and restart once LFTs normalize
Stop all TB medications and initiate drug rechallenge sequentially
Switch to a rifamycin-free regimen immediately
questions.answer: Stop all TB medications and initiate drug rechallenge sequentially
questions.explanation: Sequential drug rechallenge is recommended after LFTs return to <2x ULN to identify the causative agent and resume effective therapy.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes is admitted with fever, cough, and dyspnea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Sputum culture grows Legionella pneumophila. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Macrolides (e.g., azithromycin) are first-line for Legionella pneumonia; fluoroquinolones are alternatives, but ceftriaxone and vancomycin lack activity.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fever, chills, and a new cardiac murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following valves is MOST commonly affected in this patient population?
questions.explanation: IV drug users are at high risk for tricuspid valve endocarditis due to direct inoculation of bacteria into the venous system.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old female with a history of penicillin allergy (rash) requires treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. Sputum culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate alternative agent?
questions.explanation: Macrolides (e.g., clarithromycin) provide coverage for penicillin-susceptible S. pneumoniae in patients with non-anaphylactic penicillin allergies.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with a 2-week history of fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a right upper lobe infiltrate. Sputum smear is positive for acid-fast bacilli. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Empiric TB therapy should be initiated in patients with high clinical suspicion (e.g., AFB-positive sputum and typical radiographic findings) while awaiting culture confirmation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of COPD is admitted with severe community-acquired pneumonia. He is started on empiric therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. On day 2, his oxygen requirements increase, and he develops hypotension requiring vasopressors. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Switch to meropenem for broader coverage
Obtain blood cultures and reassess therapy
questions.answer: Obtain blood cultures and reassess therapy
questions.explanation: Clinical deterioration in CAP warrants reassessment, including blood cultures and consideration of broader-spectrum therapy if sepsis or resistant organisms are suspected.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female with a history of recurrent UTIs is started on nitrofurantoin for a culture-proven E. coli UTI. Which of the following is the MOST important monitoring parameter during therapy?
questions.explanation: Nitrofurantoin is renally eliminated; monitoring serum creatinine ensures adequate drug levels and avoids toxicity in patients with renal impairment.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30 mL/min) is admitted with pneumonia. Local antibiogram shows high resistance of Klebsiella pneumoniae to ceftriaxone. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Ertapenem provides broad-spectrum coverage for gram-negative organisms, including ESBL-producing Klebsiella, and is less nephrotoxic than other carbapenems in CKD.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4 150 cells/mm³) presents with fever, cough, and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows diffuse infiltrates. Which of the following is the MOST likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is a common opportunistic infection in HIV patients with CD4 counts <200 cells/mm³.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female with a history of penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis) is admitted with cellulitis. The organism is identified as methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is the preferred agent for MSSA in patients with severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis) due to lack of cross-reactivity.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use is admitted with fever and a new cardiac murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus epidermidis. Which of the following is the MOST likely source of infection?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common cause of catheter-related bloodstream infections in IV drug users due to biofilm formation on indwelling devices.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of diabetes and chronic kidney disease is admitted with a diabetic foot infection. Wound culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Piperacillin-tazobactam provides broad-spectrum coverage for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common pathogen in diabetic foot infections.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female with a history of asthma is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. Sputum culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin is the first-line therapy for penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae in patients without severe penicillin allergy.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of COPD is admitted with an acute exacerbation. He is started on empiric therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanate. On day 3, he develops watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a high-risk agent for C. difficile infection; symptoms of diarrhea and abdominal cramping are classic for this complication.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male with a history of tuberculosis presents with fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a right upper lobe cavity. Sputum culture grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistant to isoniazid and rifampin. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Resistance to isoniazid and rifampin (MDR-TB) requires a tailored regimen with at least four second-line drugs based on susceptibility testing.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female with a history of penicillin allergy (rash) is admitted with meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Gram stain shows gram-positive diplococci. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone provides coverage for penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae in patients with non-anaphylactic penicillin allergies; vancomycin is added if resistance is suspected.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male with a history of alcohol use disorder is admitted with fever, cough, and dyspnea. Chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation. Sputum culture grows Klebsiella pneumoniae. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Piperacillin-tazobactam provides broad-spectrum coverage for Klebsiella pneumoniae, including ESBL-producing strains, which are common in alcohol use disorder.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old female with a history of hypertension and diabetes is admitted with fever, cough, and dyspnea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Sputum culture grows Legionella pneumophila. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Macrolides (e.g., azithromycin) are first-line for Legionella pneumonia; fluoroquinolones are alternatives, but ceftriaxone and vancomycin lack activity.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fever, chills, and a new cardiac murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is the preferred agent for MSSA in patients with severe penicillin allergy or IV drug use history due to reliable coverage and reduced risk of resistance.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female with a history of recurrent UTIs is started on nitrofurantoin for a culture-proven E. coli UTI. Which of the following is the MOST important counseling point regarding adverse effects?
options: Take with food to reduce nausea
Report any signs of pulmonary toxicity
questions.answer: Report any signs of pulmonary toxicity
questions.explanation: Nitrofurantoin can cause acute or chronic pulmonary toxicity; patients should be counseled to report cough, dyspnea, or fever promptly.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of COPD is admitted with an acute exacerbation. He is started on empiric therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. On day 2, his oxygen requirements increase, and he develops hypotension requiring vasopressors. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Switch to meropenem for broader coverage
Obtain blood cultures and reassess therapy
questions.answer: Obtain blood cultures and reassess therapy
questions.explanation: Clinical deterioration in CAP warrants reassessment, including blood cultures and consideration of broader-spectrum therapy if sepsis or resistant organisms are suspected.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes is admitted with fever, cough, and dyspnea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Sputum culture grows Legionella pneumophila. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Macrolides (e.g., azithromycin) are first-line for Legionella pneumonia; fluoroquinolones are alternatives, but ceftriaxone and vancomycin lack activity.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use is admitted with fever, chills, and a new cardiac murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus epidermidis. Which of the following is the MOST likely source of infection?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common cause of catheter-related bloodstream infections in IV drug users due to biofilm formation on indwelling devices.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30 mL/min) is admitted with pneumonia. Local antibiogram shows high resistance of Klebsiella pneumoniae to ceftriaxone. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Ertapenem provides broad-spectrum coverage for gram-negative organisms, including ESBL-producing Klebsiella, and is less nephrotoxic than other carbapenems in CKD.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4 150 cells/mm³) presents with fever, cough, and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows diffuse infiltrates. Which of the following is the MOST likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is a common opportunistic infection in HIV patients with CD4 counts <200 cells/mm³.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female with a history of penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis) is admitted with cellulitis. The organism is identified as methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is the preferred agent for MSSA in patients with severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis) due to lack of cross-reactivity.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of COPD is admitted with an acute exacerbation. He is started on empiric therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanate. On day 3, he develops watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a high-risk agent for C. difficile infection; symptoms of diarrhea and abdominal cramping are classic for this complication.

questions.stem: List four (4) minor manifestations of acute rheumatic fever according to the Jones criteria.
questions.modelAnswer: 1. Fever; 2. Arthralgia (without arthritis); 3. Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP); 4. Prolonged PR interval on electrocardiogram.

questions.stem: Outline four (4) symptoms and signs that should raise suspicion of viral pharyngitis.
questions.modelAnswer: 1. Cough; 2. Coryza (nasal congestion/runny nose); 3. Conjunctivitis; 4. Absence of fever or low-grade fever; 5. Presence of viral exanthem or oral ulcers.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male with a history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis 3 years ago presents with 3 weeks of malaise, night sweats, and 5 kg weight loss. Sputum GeneXpert is positive for rifampicin-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Identify the diagnosis and design a five-drug treatment plan for this patient.
questions.modelAnswer: Diagnosis: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Treatment plan: 1. Levofloxacin; 2. Bedaquiline; 3. Linezolid; 4. Clofazimine; 5. Pyrazinamide (or cycloserine if pyrazinamide-resistant). Duration: 18–24 months with directly observed therapy (DOT).

questions.stem: Describe six (6) core elements of an antimicrobial stewardship program.
questions.modelAnswer: 1. Leadership commitment; 2. Accountability (designated stewardship leader); 3. Pharmacy expertise; 4. Action (e.g., preauthorization, prospective audit and feedback); 5. Tracking (antibiotic use and resistance patterns); 6. Reporting (to clinicians and hospital leadership); 7. Education (of clinicians and patients).

questions.stem:
A 22-year-old university student is brought to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of fever, headache, and neck stiffness. On examination, she is confused, has a temperature of 39.5°C, a heart rate of 120 bpm, and a blood pressure of 90/50 mmHg. Petechial rash is noted on her trunk and extremities. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 13.  

(a) Identify the most probable diagnosis and the likely causative organism. (2 marks)  
(b) Justify your answer in (a) above. (3 marks)  
(c) Describe three (3) investigations you would recommend to support your diagnosis. (3 marks)  
(d) Review five (5) patient-related factors to consider when selecting empirical antimicrobial therapy. (5 marks)  
(e) Propose an appropriate treatment plan for this patient. (4 marks)  
(f) List two (2) complications you would be worried about in this patient. (1 mark)  
(g) Explain how you would manage the contacts of this patient. (2 marks)

modelAnswer.a: Diagnosis: Meningococcal meningitis. Likely causative organism: Neisseria meningitidis.
modelAnswer.b: The triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status is classic for meningitis. The petechial rash is highly suggestive of meningococcemia, caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which invades the bloodstream and meninges.
modelAnswer.c: 1. Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis (cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture); 2. Blood cultures; 3. PCR for Neisseria meningitidis from blood or CSF.
modelAnswer.d: 1. Age and immune status (young adults are at higher risk); 2. Hemodynamic instability (septic shock requiring vasopressors); 3. Presence of rash (suggests disseminated intravascular coagulation); 4. Renal function (risk of acute kidney injury); 5. Allergies or prior adverse drug reactions.
modelAnswer.e: Empirical therapy: IV ceftriaxone 2g q12h (or IV chloramphenicol 1g q6h if penicillin-allergic). Add IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h for 4 days to reduce inflammation. Supportive care: IV fluids, vasopressors if needed, and close monitoring in ICU.
modelAnswer.f: 1. Septic shock with multi-organ failure; 2. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
modelAnswer.g: Close contacts (e.g., household members, intimate contacts) should receive chemoprophylaxis with oral ciprofloxacin 500mg single dose or rifampicin 600mg q12h for 2 days. Vaccination should be considered for close contacts if the strain is vaccine-preventable.

questions.stem:
Mr. JW, a 42-year-old male, presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, cough producing rusty sputum, pleuritic chest pain, and sudden onset of dyspnea. He returned from a conference 5 days ago where he frequently used whirlpool baths. On examination, his temperature is 38.8°C, respiratory rate is 33/min, SpO2 is 85% on room air, blood pressure is 100/68 mmHg, and heart rate is 110 bpm. Urea is 8.5 mmol/L.  

(a) Identify the most likely diagnosis and the most likely causative organism. (2 marks)  
(b) Justify your answer in (a) above. (6 points @0.5 marks each)  
(c) Outline two (2) additional investigations you would recommend. (2 marks)  
(d) Evaluate whether you would recommend treating this patient as an outpatient, inpatient (general ward), or in an intensive care unit. Justify your answer. (4 marks)  
(e) Formulate a treatment plan for this patient. (5 marks)  
(f) Using appropriate examples, examine how you would monitor for response to treatment. (4 marks)

modelAnswer.a: Diagnosis: Legionella pneumonia. Likely causative organism: Legionella pneumophila.
modelAnswer.b: 1. Exposure to whirlpool baths (risk factor for Legionella); 2. Sudden onset of high fever and systemic symptoms; 3. Rusty sputum and pleuritic chest pain; 4. Hypoxemia and tachypnea (severe CAP); 5. Elevated urea (suggests dehydration or sepsis); 6. Absence of typical CAP pathogens on Gram stain.
modelAnswer.c: 1. Legionella urinary antigen test; 2. Chest X-ray or CT scan to assess extent of pneumonia and complications (e.g., empyema).
modelAnswer.d: Admission to ICU is warranted due to severe CAP with hypoxemia (SpO2 85%), tachypnea (RR 33/min), hypotension (BP 100/68 mmHg), and elevated urea (8.5 mmol/L), indicating high risk of respiratory failure and septic shock.
modelAnswer.e: Treatment plan: IV azithromycin 500mg daily for 7–10 days (or IV levofloxacin 750mg daily if macrolide-intolerant). Add IV ceftriaxone 2g daily empirically for atypical and typical coverage until Legionella is confirmed. Supportive care: supplemental oxygen, IV fluids, and close monitoring for sepsis.
modelAnswer.f: Monitoring: 1. Clinical parameters (temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation); 2. Microbiological clearance (repeat sputum cultures or Legionella urinary antigen if initially positive); 3. Laboratory parameters (CRP, WBC count, urea, electrolytes); 4. Radiological improvement (repeat chest X-ray in 48–72 hours).
